cluePool.definition: A methodology focused on iterative development, flexibility, and delivering value quickly
The programs, data, and instructions that tell a computer what to do
The complete process of designing, writing, testing, and maintaining software
The specific needs, features, and constraints requested by the user or client
The application of science and math to design and build complex systems
The high-level structural design of a software system and its components
The process of defining the look, functionality, and structure of a system
Reusable, standard solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design
A specific state or numbered release of a software product
The management and tracking of changes made to code or documents
A set of interconnected components forming a complex whole
Happening without interruption; a type of integration where code is merged frequently
The process of combining separate software modules into a single system
A procedure to evaluate the quality, performance, or reliability of software
Guided or controlled by a specific principle (e.g., 'Test-______ development')
A self-contained entity in code that bundles data and the methods that operate on that data
Aligned or focused around a particular concept (e.g., 'Object-________ programming')
The process of writing instructions that tell a computer how to perform a task
The instructions written in a specific language to be executed by a computer
Restructuring existing computer code to improve its readability or structure without changing its behavior
The standard of something as measured against good criteria; how good or bad software is
A promise or guarantee; a process to ensure software meets standards (Quality ________)
The process of updating, fixing, and keeping software in good working condition after release
The period of time something exists; the first word in SDLC (Software Development ____ Cycle)
A series of events that are regularly repeated in the same order
A formal assessment or examination of code by peers to find bugs or improve quality
The person who interacts with or operates the final software product
In Agile, a short, simple description of a feature told from the perspective of the person who desires it (User _______)
The process of finding and fixing errors or defects in software
A temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product or service
The process of organizing, planning, and directing resources to achieve a goal
An error, flaw, or fault in a computer program that causes it to produce an incorrect result
A structured set of data held in a computer, usually accessed electronically
A set of rules that allows different software applications to communicate with each other (Application Programming Interface)
To move software from a development environment into a live production environment
A short, time-boxed period in Agile when a scrum team works to complete a set amount of work
A separate, independent unit of software that can be developed and tested in isolation
A pre-built structure of code that developers can use to build applications faster
A single piece of work that needs to be completed as part of a larger project
The act of monitoring the progress of tasks, bugs, or features
A detailed proposal for doing or achieving something in the future
A group of people working together towards a common goal
A flaw or imperfection in software that causes it to fail
A distinctive attribute or aspect of a software product
A version of software made available to users
The original code written by a programmer before it is compiled (_____ code)
The process of converting source code files into standalone software artifacts
The reasoning conducted or assessed according to strict principles of validity in code
Raw, unprocessed facts, measurements, or observations
A series of actions or steps taken to achieve a particular end
A mistake in the code that causes the program to behave incorrectly
A representation of a system or process, often used in software design
A linear data structure that follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle
The fundamental physical and organizational structures and facilities (such as power grids, water supplies, transportation, and telecommunications) needed for a country to function.
Essential public services supplied to homes and businesses, such as electricity, water, natural gas, and sewage systems.
Integrated networks of hardware (physical equipment) and software that process data and automate control of processes or devices.
Embedded software specifically designed to monitor, manage, and regulate the physical operation of equipment or machinery (e.g., in cars, appliances, or industrial robots).
The large-scale production of goods using machinery, tools, and processing techniques in factories.
The process and logistics of transporting, storing, and delivering goods from manufacturers to retailers or consumers.
Converted to, or operated by, automated computer systems rather than manual labor or non-electronic equipment.
The network of institutions (banks, stock exchanges, insurance companies) and markets that allow the flow, exchange, and management of money and investments globally.
Systems, applications, or industries where software plays a dominant, critical, or major role in their design, operation, and delivery of value.
The systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to designing, developing, testing, maintaining, and managing software applications and systems.
Collections of interconnected software programs, algorithms, and data structures working together to perform complex functions or solve specific problems.
Existing as a concept, idea, or logical structure rather than as a concrete, physical object.
Unable to be touched, seen, or physically grasped; having no physical body or substance.
Restricted, limited, or forced to operate within specific boundaries or rules.
The inherent physical, chemical, or mechanical characteristics of tangible matter (such as weight, density, flexibility, or heat tolerance).
The fundamental principles of nature governing the material universe, such as gravity, thermodynamics, and conservation of energy.
The physical methods and steps used to mass-produce tangible hardware or goods from raw materials.
The systematic, disciplined application of engineering principles and practices to the design, development, testing, and maintenance of software.
Physical or biological boundaries imposed by nature (such as the speed of light, maximum material strength, or finite physical space).
Real-world material restrictions (like size, weight, heat dissipation, or wear and tear) that limit what can be physically built.
Composed of many interconnected and interdependent parts, making a system difficult to analyze, predict, or fully comprehend.
Requiring significant time, financial resources, labor, or risk of introducing new bugs when attempting to modify or update the system.
Specialized computer systems built directly inside larger mechanical or electrical devices (such as cars, medical equipment, or home appliances) to perform dedicated, specific tasks.
Large-scale, distributed software networks that process, manage, and share massive amounts of data globally across the internet or private networks (e.g., cloud services, global banking systems).
Standardized symbols, diagrams, or modeling languages (like UML) that attempt to provide a single, globally understood language for designing software.
Structured, step-by-step frameworks or methodologies (like Agile or Waterfall) that guide how software development projects are planned and executed.
Specific, hands-on procedures, algorithms, or practical skills that engineers use to solve particular problems during coding or testing.
The disciplined application of engineering principles to the design, creation, testing, and maintenance of software.
Large-scale software built to support business operations, data tracking, and decision-making within a company or enterprise (e.g., payroll, inventory, or customer relationship management systems).
Specialized software designed to precisely monitor, command, and regulate physical laboratory or scientific hardware (such as a telescope or spectrometer).
Video games that require advanced processing power and real-time computation to render complex 3D visual environments, physics simulations, and animations smoothly.
